items.text: WTI is at $89.53/bbl and Brent at $92.94/bbl, which sits higher than 78% of readings over the past five years, and the trend across recent observations is falling. Energy is the single largest swing factor behind headline inflation volatility, which means it feeds directly into the Fed's reaction function and therefore into your base-rate assumptions. On the portfolio side, sustained moves here reset input costs for transport-, logistics-, chemicals- and manufacturing-exposed borrowers, and are worth stress-testing in any credit model that assumed energy costs stay near recent levels.

Payrolls added +165K in the latest report, against a +137K average across the last three readings, and unemployment stands at 4.1%. Weekly initial claims are running near 203K, with average hourly earnings up 3.1% year over year. Hiring momentum is the most reliable leading read on demand durability for growth-oriented credits: payroll deceleration typically shows up in borrower topline growth and covenant headroom a quarter or two before it appears in the credit metrics themselves. Wage growth running above pre-pandemic norms also keeps services inflation sticky, which matters for labor-intensive issuers where payroll is the dominant variable cost.

Headline CPI is running 3.7% year over year (+0.4pt versus the prior reading), with core CPI at 2.6% and core PCE — the metric the FOMC actually targets — at 3.1%. Producer prices are up 6.5% year over year, the earliest read on what is coming at borrower input costs. The central tension is the gap between volatile headline prints, which are largely energy-driven and mean-revert, and the stickier core measures that determine the policy path. For underwriting, the practical implication is to price to sticky rather than falling financing costs until core decelerates convincingly, and to watch pricing power closely at issuers absorbing input-cost inflation they cannot pass through.

The Fed funds target stands at 3.75–4.00%, the 10-year Treasury at 4.92% and the 2-year at 4.63%. The 10Y-minus-2Y curve sits at +29bp, holding its normal upward slope, which is generally constructive for credit: it is not pricing imminent recession and it widens the margin banks and direct lenders earn borrowing short and lending long. The front end is your fastest read on repricing of hike-versus-cut odds around each CPI, PCE and jobs print, while the long end drives enterprise valuations and refinancing math. Every floating-rate structure in the book keys off the short end, so a persistent move here changes the cost-of-capital assumption underneath new originations mid-process.

High-yield OAS is 376bp, wider than 96% of the past five years, and rising across recent observations. Investment-grade OAS is 98bp. Index spreads are the cleanest market-priced gauge of how much you are actually being paid for credit risk. The pattern worth watching for special situations sourcing is compression at the index level masking widening dispersion underneath: idiosyncratic stress tends to surface in specific issuers — leveraged, tariff-exposed, or facing near-term maturities — well before the benchmark moves. That dispersion, not the index level, is where the opportunity set originates.

Real GDP grew 3.4% (QoQ SAAR) in the most recent quarter and the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow is tracking +3.2% for the current quarter, an early read ahead of the official advance estimate. Below-trend but positive growth is the backdrop that supports growth-oriented positioning over distressed or turnaround exposure. A material downside surprise would shift the opportunity set the other way, toward stressed and special situations, so the gap between the nowcast and the official print is worth tracking as an early warning rather than waiting on the lagging release.

University of Michigan consumer sentiment is 48.0, lower than 98% of readings over the past five years, and the personal saving rate is 3.8%. Housing starts are running 1.31M SAAR against a 7.28% 30-year mortgage rate. Housing and the consumer are the most rate-sensitive parts of the demand picture and typically the first to register policy tightening. A low saving rate means spending is running ahead of income growth, which is durable while labor income holds but drains quickly if payroll growth decelerates — worth tracking alongside the jobs data for consumer-facing and housing-cycle-exposed borrowers.

themeCards.title: Credit Stress in Speculative Grade
themeCards.statusLine: CCC spreads exploded 51 bps WoW to 1361 bps; ninth straight month of ISM Prices Paid >70 squeezes cash flow. Covenant waivers and restructuring risk rising into year-end refinancing wall.
themeCards.relevance: Distressed credit dislocations and event-driven opportunities in lower-rated bonds, CLOs, and CDS are materially more fertile. Special situations portfolio tilts (short duration, long recovery value, long credits trading on fundamentals) are warranted.

themeCards.title: China Slowdown & Export Demand Risk
themeCards.statusLine: Official NBS Manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 in Oct (below 50 contraction threshold), down from 50.1 in Sept, citing seasonal factors and demand moderation. SME PMI deteriorated sharply to 47.5. This threatens US export growth and EM FX stability.
themeCards.relevance: EM credit (corporates with China exposure, Asian local currency debt) faces demand headwinds; US multinationals with high China revenue face earnings risk. Chinese sovereign credit and policy pivots are key barometers for dislocations in Asian credit markets and cross-border refi conditions.

themeCards.title: Manufacturing Pricing Power vs Demand Inflection
themeCards.statusLine: ISM Mfg PMI at 55.5 (beat) but respondent sentiment worsened 66% negative (up from prior months); Prices Paid at 75.2 for ninth straight month. Iran war, tariffs, supply chain stress cited. Output strong but pricing sustainability uncertain if input costs roll over.
themeCards.relevance: Margin compression risk for leveraged manufacturers; refinance risk for capex-dependent issuers (machinery, transportation equipment). Watch for negative guidance revisions and covenant stress. Special situations investors should track leverage multiples and refinancing maturities in cyclical industrials.

themeCards.title: Residential Housing Market Stress
themeCards.statusLine: Existing home sales plunged to 3.75M (Oct) from 3.97M (Sept); mortgage rates at 7.28%. Housing starts improved to 1309k but far below demographic need. Affordability crisis persists despite consumer sentiment bounce, flagging demand destruction.
themeCards.relevance: RMBS and MBS spreads remain vulnerable; REITs and homebuilders face refinance and covenant pressure. Watch for mortgage delinquency upticks and loan loss reserve guidance. Mortgage servicers and sub-prime auto lenders in distressed credit baskets are relevant special situations plays.

themeCards.title: Fed Holding While Inflation Sticky
themeCards.statusLine: Fed at 4.0%, curve flat, 10y/2y at 29 bps. Core CPI/PCE sticky (2.57% / 3.12% through Sept); PPI at 6.52% (Oct). Markets now price 94% odds of ECB 25 bp hike Dec 17. Divergence widens policy uncertainty and FX vol.
themeCards.relevance: Reinvestment risk and bond carry/roll-down asymmetry flatten. Cross-currency basis widening supports EM hard-currency credit spreads, but refinance risk rises for FX-mismatched entities. Fed's policy patience conflicts with ECB tightening, creating tactical windows in relative value and hedging strategies for multi-jurisdiction credit portfolios.

themeCards.title: Covenant Tightening Ahead of Year-End Refinancing
themeCards.statusLine: Widening spreads, elevated VIX (28.44), and CCC distress signal refinancing stress. Maturity ladder for BB and B-rated issuers concentrates in Q4 2026 and Q1 2027. Covenant definitions and waiver prevalence rising.
themeCards.relevance: Direct special situations opportunity: distressed exchange offers, covenant waivers, restructuring advisory, and long bonds of issuers facing refinance stress are rich with event catalysts. Monitor redemption calendars and rating agency negative watches.
